stories.blurb: On November 20, 1776, a day after the British took Fort Lee, Washington rode into Hackensack and his army camped on the Green. He worked from Peter Zabriskie's house and chose to keep retreating, which set up the Battle of Trenton weeks later.

stories.title: The Hiss That Would Not Go Away
stories.blurb: The horn antenna in Holmdel was built in 1959, on Crawford Hill, for a space project called Echo. Echo used giant shiny balloons in orbit to bounce radio signals from one place on Earth to another. The horn was made of aluminum, about fifty feet long, with an opening twenty feet square, and it weighed around eighteen tons. By 1962, Bell Labs no longer needed it for Echo. So it was handed to a radio astronomer named Arno Penzias, and Robert Wilson was hired to help. They wanted to measure faint radio signals from the Milky Way. To do that, they first had to clear out every bit of noise in the system. But there was a steady hiss they could not get rid of. They checked everything. At one point they even suspected pigeon droppings inside the horn, so they shooed the birds away and cleaned it out. The hiss stayed. Then they heard that a team at Princeton, led by Robert Dicke, had been working out a theory. If the universe began in a hot Big Bang, there should be a faint leftover glow everywhere. Dicke sent them a draft of his group's paper. The hiss was not coming from the horn. It was coming from the universe. Both teams published back to back in the Astrophysical Journal in 1965. The discovery was the final blow to the rival steady-state idea of the universe. Penzias and Wilson had not been looking for the Big Bang. They shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1978.

stories.title: The Puritans Who Built Newark
stories.blurb: Newark began in May of 1666, when a band of Puritan families from Connecticut landed on the shore of the Passaic River and began building. Their leader was Captain Robert Treat. Treat had been born in England, settled in Milford, and became a local magistrate. The group came from the New Haven Colony, and they left for a reason. New Haven had been merged with a more liberal neighbor, Connecticut. The Puritans of New Haven wanted to keep political power in the hands of members of their own church. Under the merger, they were about to lose that power to people outside their church. So they moved to New Jersey and built a town where they could run things their way. In Newark, Treat became the town's magistrate and town clerk. He is said to have helped lay out Broad Street, still the widest street in the city. The church at the center of the settlement is today's Old First Church, on Broad Street near Branford, the mother church of New Jersey Presbyterians.

stories.blurb: In October of 1928, Newark opened the first major airport in the New York area. The city built it on sixty-eight acres of marshland. It grew fast. The Port Authority says it quickly became the world's busiest commercial airport. The National Park Service says that in the early years, one-third of the world's air traffic passed down its runways. During World War Two the Army Air Corps ran it. In 1948, the Port Authority took over, and it added an instrument runway, a terminal building, a control tower and an air cargo center. Today it is Newark Liberty International, owned by the cities of Newark and Elizabeth.

stories.title: Everything in Newark Was for Sale
stories.blurb: Hugh Addonizio was the mayor of Newark from 1962 to 1970. Before that, he served in Congress. In 1970, a federal jury found him and four other defendants guilty on sixty-four counts, sixty-three of extortion and one of conspiracy. He was convicted of sharing in $1.5 million in extorted kickbacks from contractors on city water and sewer lines. On September 22, 1970, the judge, George Barlow, sentenced Addonizio to ten years in prison and a $25,000 fine. He said the crimes had torn at the very heart of our civilized society and our form of representative government. Addonizio served sixty-two months and died in 1981. One of the prosecutors, Garrett Brown Jr., later said there was a sense that everything in Newark was for sale at the time, and it was.

stories.title: Six Days in July, 1967
stories.blurb: On July 12, 1967, Newark police arrested a Black cab driver named John Smith, after he drove around a police car and double-parked. Civil rights leaders saw that he was hurt and demanded he go to a hospital. Rumors spread that he had died. That night, crowds gathered outside the Fourth Precinct. After midnight, Molotov cocktails were thrown at the building. At two-twenty in the morning, Mayor Hugh Addonizio asked Governor Richard Hughes to send in the National Guard. More than three thousand Guardsmen and five hundred state troopers came into the city. The violence lasted until July 17. Twenty-six people were killed, and hundreds were hurt. It was the worst civil disorder in New Jersey history. Historians point to causes that had built for years. Residents of the Central Ward feared losing their homes to a planned medical school on a hundred and fifty acres. And there were repeated complaints of police misconduct.

stories.title: The Cherry Trees of Branch Brook Park
stories.blurb: Branch Brook Park in Newark was the first county park in the United States. It is nearly four miles long, and it is named for a small brook that ran through the valley to the Passaic River. The famous Olmsted landscape firm began designing it in 1898. The cherry trees came later. Caroline Bamberger Fuld, whose brother ran Bamberger's Department Store, had seen the cherry blossoms in Washington, D.C. She set out to create a display in Essex County that would rival the capital's. The plan was drawn up in 1928, with about twenty-two hundred trees of more than twenty kinds. The planting was finished in 1932. Today the park has more than four thousand cherry trees, more in number and variety than Washington's display, according to Essex County Parks. At its height, the blossom festival draws more than ten thousand people a day.

stories.title: The Man Who Made Patent Leather
stories.blurb: Seth Boyden was born on a farm in Massachusetts in 1788 and moved to Newark in the 1810s. He became one of America's great early inventors. In 1819 he copied a secret European method of putting a glossy lacquer on leather. He set up the first factory in the United States to make patent leather, the shiny stuff of dress shoes. Then, in 1826, after six years of trying, he produced his first casting of malleable iron, a tough iron that bends instead of breaking. The Franklin Institute honored him for it two years later. He also built locomotives and steam engines, and he is credited with making the first daguerreotype in the United States. But he cared little about getting rich. He moved on to new experiments instead.

stories.title: The Ironbound and Ferry Street
stories.blurb: Ferry Street in Newark's Ironbound is a mile long, and it started as a road for ferries. In 1765 the colonial legislature chartered it as Old Ferry Road, to connect the ferries bringing goods from Manhattan and Jersey City to Newark's market. Ever since, it has been a landing place for newcomers, first Portuguese and Spanish, and more recently people from across Latin America. Since the 1970s, its Portuguese and Spanish restaurants have drawn visitors from all over. Within one block you can find Spanish paella, Brazilian rodizio, Portuguese custard tarts and Ecuadorian ceviche. One of the best-known places, Fornos of Spain, opened nearly a hundred years ago as a small pizzeria called Cortese, according to nj.com. In the 1970s a Portuguese family bought it and renamed it Fornos, Portuguese for ovens. In 1980, two new owners added "of Spain." People still go for the patatas bravas and the grilled octopus.

stories.title: Whitney Houston's Newark
stories.blurb: Whitney Houston was born in Newark on August 9, 1963. Her mother was the gospel and soul singer Cissy Houston, and her cousin was Dionne Warwick. She grew up singing at New Hope Baptist Church in Newark. Her family moved to East Orange when she was seven, but the church stayed her musical home. At fourteen, at the Town Hall, she got her first standing ovation for a solo. In 1983, Arista Records signed her. The New Jersey Hall of Fame says she went on to sell more than two hundred million recordings and win eight Grammy Awards. It was a long way from the choir loft in Newark.

stories.title: Longie Zwillman, King of Newark's Underworld
stories.blurb: Abner Zwillman, called Longie, became one of the most powerful underworld figures in the country. During Prohibition he smuggled whiskey into New Jersey. In 1956 he was tried for income tax evasion, but the jury deadlocked. Afterward, several of his associates were charged with trying to bribe jurors. On February 26, 1959, he was found dead at his home in West Orange. He was fifty-four. There is another side to his story. From 1933 to 1941, he founded a group called the New Jersey Minutemen, an anti-fascist group that fought the pro-Nazi German American Bund in Newark.

stories.title: How Alexander Hamilton Founded Paterson
stories.blurb: In 1791, Alexander Hamilton helped start the Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures, called S.U.M. It was a company backed by wealthy New Jersey investors, and its goal was to make goods in America. Hamilton had sent his Report on Manufactures to Congress on December 5, 1791, and that report was the spark for the society. The charter was drawn up and revised by Hamilton himself. The place they chose was the Great Falls of the Passaic River. In May of 1792, the society bought seven hundred acres above and below the falls. That purchase created the city of Paterson. The first raceway, a channel to carry water from the falls to the mills, was built in early 1794. The city was named for William Paterson, the second governor of New Jersey. It later became known as Silk City.

stories.title: Twenty-Five Thousand Silk Workers on Strike
stories.blurb: The Great Falls powered Paterson's mills, which produced nearly half of the silk in the United States. In February of 1913, the broad-silk weavers walked out. The owners wanted each worker to run four looms instead of two. Soon about twenty-five thousand workers had shut down roughly three hundred silk mills and dye houses. The strike lasted almost five months. The workers brought in organizers from the Industrial Workers of the World, including Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, Carlo Tresca and Bill Haywood. The strike headquarters was the home of Pietro Botto, and speakers addressed crowds from the second-floor porch. On June 7, more than a thousand strikers performed a pageant about the strike at Madison Square Garden in New York. But the strike was defeated, and the workers' demands were not met. Even so, the owners held back the four-loom system for another ten years.

stories.title: Hinchliffe Stadium and Larry Doby
stories.blurb: Hinchliffe Stadium in Paterson was named for Mayor John Hinchliffe. It opened on July 8, 1932. It became a home for Negro Leagues baseball, and the New York Black Yankees made it their home ground. In 1933, a game billed as the Colored Championship of the Nation was played there, and the Philadelphia Stars beat the Black Yankees. Stars who played there included Josh Gibson, Monte Irvin and Satchel Paige. And one of the players was a local. Larry Doby, from Paterson, became the first African American player in the American League in July of 1947. The Baseball Hall of Fame inducted him in 1998.

stories.title: The Submarine in the Passaic River
stories.blurb: John Philip Holland was born in Ireland in 1841. He moved to the United States in 1873 and soon came to Paterson to teach math at St. John's. He had a dream: a boat that could travel under the water. In the spring of 1878, his first boat, Holland One, was moved to Paterson. It was fourteen feet long and weighed about two and a quarter tons. He tested it in the Passaic River, launching from a boathouse above the Great Falls. On June 6, 1878, it made two runs completely underwater, at a depth of twelve feet. Afterward, the boat was sunk in the river. It lay on the bottom until 1927, when it was found and raised. Today it sits in the Paterson Museum, along with his second prototype. Navies around the world later adopted the modern submarine his work led to.

stories.title: The Colt Revolver Was Born in Paterson
stories.blurb: In 1836, Samuel Colt got a patent for a revolving pistol. To build it, he organized the Patent Arms Manufacturing Company, and he put its factory in Paterson, right below the Great Falls of the Passaic River. The Paterson works made revolving rifles first, and then the Colt Paterson revolver. It had a trigger that folded out of sight until the hammer was cocked. It was the first commercially made repeating handgun tied to Colt's name. But the business did not last. The company had failed by 1842, and the Paterson factory stopped making guns. Colt's comeback came later, when Captain Samuel Walker suggested improvements and ordered one thousand revolvers, and Colt moved production to a factory belonging to Eli Whitney Junior.

stories.title: Rubin "Hurricane" Carter, Convicted and Freed
stories.blurb: Rubin Carter was born in Clifton, New Jersey, in 1937, and grew up in Paterson. At about two-thirty in the morning on June 17, 1966, three people were shot at the Lafayette Bar and Grill in Paterson. Shortly afterward, police stopped a car carrying Carter and a young man named John Artis. In 1967, a jury convicted both men of murder, and they were given life sentences. In 1976, Bob Dylan wrote a song about the case, called "Hurricane." In 1985, a federal judge, H. Lee Sarokin, overturned the convictions, citing prosecutors' misconduct and dubious eyewitness testimony. Prosecutors declined to try the case again, and Carter walked free that November at the age of forty-eight.

stories.title: New Jersey's First Capital
stories.blurb: Elizabeth is called New Jersey's first city. In 1664, English settlers bought a large piece of land between the Raritan and Passaic rivers from the local Indigenous people. They paid in trade goods such as wampum, cloth and tools. By 1665, there was a growing village there called Elizabethtown, named in honor of Lady Elizabeth Carteret. Under Philip Carteret, it became New Jersey's first capital, and the colony's first legislature met there in 1668. In 1855, it was officially incorporated as the City of Elizabeth.

stories.title: The Singer Sewing Machine Factory
stories.blurb: In the early 1870s, the Singer Manufacturing Company built a huge factory on the waterfront in Elizabethport, on Newark Bay. It had begun buying land there in October of 1870. On October 18, 1873, Singer moved all of its United States manufacturing there. One source calls it the largest factory in the world devoted to a single product. By 1876, Singer was making more sewing machines than all of its American competitors combined. By 1912, it had about ninety percent of the world market, according to the federal Historic American Engineering Record. During the First World War, the plant even made cannons and pistols. A court record says the workforce reached about ten thousand at its peak. In February of 1982, Singer announced it would close the plant.

stories.title: The Shot at Connecticut Farms
stories.blurb: In June of 1780, British and Hessian troops landed at Elizabethtown, planning to march toward Morristown, where George Washington's army was camped. Their target was the camp itself. They had to pass through Connecticut Farms, now part of Union. There, about fifteen hundred Continental soldiers and militia, led by General William Maxwell, fought them. During the fighting, Hannah Caldwell, the wife of the local minister, Reverend James Caldwell, stayed in her house with her younger children, a nurse and a friend. According to the accounts, a soldier fired through the window and killed her. Her death increased the resolve of the colonists to keep fighting. Sixteen days later, at the Battle of Springfield, the British tried again. When the American soldiers ran short of paper for their muskets, Reverend Caldwell gathered hymnals, and the soldiers used the pages. The British retreated, after burning Springfield.

stories.title: Boxwood Hall
stories.blurb: Boxwood Hall in Elizabeth was built around 1750 by Samuel Woodruff, who was then the mayor of Elizabethtown. From 1772 to 1795, it was the home of Elias Boudinot, who served as President of the Continental Congress in 1782 and 1783. It was during his term, on October 31, 1783, that word reached Congress that the Treaty of Paris had been signed, officially ending the Revolutionary War. A young Alexander Hamilton studied in Elizabeth in 1773 and visited the house, and he and the Boudinots stayed friends for life. George Washington was a guest there too. Jonathan Dayton, the youngest signer of the Constitution, also lived in the house. In 1938, the building was threatened with demolition. Local citizens raised money to buy it and gave it to the State of New Jersey. It has been a museum since 1947.

stories.title: Judy Blume of Elizabeth
stories.blurb: Judy Blume was born in Elizabeth, New Jersey, on February 12, 1938, as Judith Sussman. Her father was a dentist. She graduated from New York University in 1961. Her first book, "The One in the Middle Is the Green Kangaroo," came out in 1969. In 1970, she published "Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret," which was controversial for dealing with serious topics, including teenage worries and religious identity. In the 1970s, thirteen of her books reached bookstores. Her 1975 young-adult book "Forever" became a frequent target of censorship. She served on the board of the National Coalition Against Censorship. The New Jersey Hall of Fame inducted her in 2010.
